rv.q: Foy and Smith manage the switches of mood and tone with a virtuosity that verges on ostentatious, and there are very few off-moments in pace.
Smith and Foy are always watchable, and ‘Lungs’ is funny throughout.
But the piece's warm personal treatment of such a serious subject is both witty and uncomfortably effective.
This is an absorbing evening not because of any large environmental claims but because of the needling but generous dialogue that takes you into the heart of a couple.
It is hard to imagine a finer outing for it than Matthew Warchus’ gleaming, ideally paced Old Vic production starring Claire Foy and Matt Smith.
The main attraction of this intoxicating evening lies in the accuracy of the depictions.

Nonetheless, these performers were skilled enough to let us sense the discomfort, doubt and resentment beneath the surface of their stoical characters. I am happy to report that Foy and Smith are equally adept at delivering such ambivalence, common to nearly all long and intimate relationships, at high volume and in equally high gear.
Overall, however, an interesting 60 minute play about the minutiae of relationships is hindered by the injection of an extra 30 minutes of dialogue about environmental issues which adds very little.
Ultimately, this is an unremarkable play that has been lavished with luxury casting – and while there's nothing uniquely demanding about these roles, it's Smith and Foy that make it worthwhile.
What could have been a static, cerebral evening turns out to be an exhilarating roller-coaster of a ride, as Foy and Smith demonstrate their undeniable chemistry and considerable acting skills.

While it is to director Matthew Warchus' credit that such continually fast pacing doesn't lead to the subject matter being brushed over without detail, it is inevitable that the play's conclusion does have a sense of feeling rushed or all too sudden.

cn.t: Foy and Smith deliver magnetic, tour-de-force performances that elevate Macmillan's intelligent but somewhat conservative two-hander about parenthood and climate anxiety, making it compellingly watchable despite occasionally scripted dialogue.
